flow.d: Room for a counterbalance truck to turn into the racks, and for pickers and the truck to pass each other.
Wider aisles leave room for fewer rows: about a fifth fewer positions than with 3 m aisles.
There are fewer pick faces than SKUs, so the slowest SKUs share a pallet position, two to a face.
The counterbalance truck can also work the dock and load trailers.
Reach-truck aisles: the truck stands in the aisle and reaches the forks out, so it needs less room than a counterbalance truck.

flow.t: Every SKU has its own face
flow.d: Enough rows for a pick face per SKU, with reserve pallets above.
Pickers and the reach truck can pass in a 3 m aisle, with care and give-way rules.
A reach truck is not built for trailers; unloading stays with pallet jacks, as in every set-up here.
A wire-guided turret truck stores pallets on both sides without turning in the aisle.
About a fifth more positions than with 3 m aisles, in the same building and height.

flow.t: One at a time in an aisle
flow.d: While the turret truck works an aisle, pickers wait outside it, and the truck waits for pickers to leave.
A man-down turret truck fetches pallets from staging itself, but loses time each trip leaving and rejoining the guide wire.
VNA needs a superflat floor in the aisles and a guide wire or rail, both paid for once, before the first pallet goes in.
